q: Which statement best describes the relationship between AI, machine learning and deep learning?
o: Deep learning is a subset of machine learning, which is a subset of AI
AI is a subset of machine learning, which is a subset of deep learning
Machine learning and deep learning are unrelated approaches to AI
Deep learning is the broadest term and includes all AI
e: AI is the broad field, ML is a way to achieve AI by learning from data, and deep learning is ML using many-layered neural networks.

q: A bank has thousands of past transactions, each labelled 'fraud' or 'not fraud'. It wants a model that labels new transactions. Which type of learning is this?
e: Labelled examples plus a known target to predict means supervised learning (here, classification).

q: A retailer wants to group customers into segments based on buying habits. It has no labels for the segments. Which approach fits?
e: Finding groups in unlabelled data is clustering, a form of unsupervised learning.

q: A company wants to predict next month's sales revenue as a number. What kind of ML problem is this?
e: Predicting a continuous number is regression. Over time it is also a forecasting problem.

q: A robot learns to walk by trying movements and receiving a reward when it stays upright. Which learning type is this?
e: Learning by trial, error and reward is reinforcement learning.

q: How are large language models usually pre-trained?
o: Self-supervised learning on large amounts of unlabelled text
Supervised learning on hand-labelled sentiment data only
Reinforcement learning with no text data
e: LLMs learn by predicting the next token in huge unlabelled text sets, so the data supplies its own labels (self-supervised). Later stages can add supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF).

q: A model scores 99% accuracy on its training data but 60% on new data. What is the most likely problem?
e: Great on training data but poor on unseen data means the model memorised rather than generalised: overfitting.
an: It's like a recipe scaler that only works for the 8 recipes it was tested on and breaks on your next new one.

q: A model performs poorly on both training data and test data. What is this called?
e: Poor on both means the model is too simple to capture the pattern: underfitting (high bias).

q: Which data split is used to judge final performance on data the model has never seen?
e: The training set teaches the model, the validation set tunes it, and the test set gives the final unbiased check.

q: Which of these is a hyperparameter rather than something the model learns?
o: The weights of a neural network
The bias values inside each neuron
e: Hyperparameters such as learning rate, epochs and batch size are set before training. Weights and biases are learned.

q: A fraud model must catch as many real fraud cases as possible, even if it raises some false alarms. Which metric matters most?
e: Recall is the share of real positives that were caught. Use it when missing a positive is costly.
an: Like a stock check that must never miss something you've run out of: a few false 'running low' warnings are fine.

q: An email filter must almost never send a real email to spam, even if some spam gets through. Which metric should be prioritised?
e: Precision is the share of flagged items that really are positive. High precision means few false alarms.
an: Same as Cooking's substitutes: only suggest a swap when you're sure it works, because a wrong substitute ruins the dish.

q: Only 1% of transactions are fraud. A model that labels everything 'not fraud' has 99% accuracy. Why is accuracy misleading here?
o: The classes are imbalanced, so accuracy hides that no fraud is caught
e: With rare classes, accuracy can look high while the model is useless. Use recall, precision, F1 or AUC instead.

q: Which metric combines precision and recall into one number?
e: F1 is the harmonic mean of precision and recall, useful when you need a balance of both.

q: Which metrics are used to evaluate a regression model? (Choose TWO.)
e: Regression predicts numbers, so you measure the size of the errors (MAE, RMSE) or explained variation (R-squared). F1, recall and confusion matrices are for classification.

q: What does a confusion matrix show?
o: Counts of true positives, false positives, true negatives and false negatives
e: A confusion matrix tabulates correct and incorrect predictions per class, from which precision and recall are calculated.

q: Which metric shows how well a binary classifier separates the two classes across all thresholds?
e: The area under the ROC curve summarises performance across every decision threshold. 1.0 is perfect, 0.5 is random.

q: After deployment, a model's accuracy slowly falls because customer behaviour has changed. What is this called?
e: When the real-world data shifts away from the training data, quality drops. Monitor for drift and retrain.
an: Your Fourth rota format changing would break the rota import the same way: the world moved, the code didn't.

q: Which AWS service detects data and model quality drift in a deployed SageMaker model?
e: SageMaker Model Monitor watches production models for data quality, model quality, bias and feature-attribution drift.

q: What is feature engineering?
o: Choosing the instance type for training
Creating and transforming input variables so the model can learn better
Writing the user interface for a model
e: Feature engineering turns raw data into useful inputs, for example extracting 'day of week' from a timestamp.

q: What is the correct order of a typical ML lifecycle?
o: Deploy, train, collect data, define problem
Define the business problem, collect and prepare data, train, evaluate, deploy, monitor
Train, define problem, monitor, collect data
e: Start from the business goal, then data, then model building, evaluation, deployment and ongoing monitoring with retraining.

q: What is MLOps?
o: Practices for automating and managing the ML lifecycle, from data to deployment and monitoring
e: MLOps applies DevOps ideas (automation, versioning, repeatable pipelines, monitoring) to ML. SageMaker Pipelines and Model Registry support it.

q: Which SageMaker feature lets business analysts build ML models with a visual, no-code interface?
e: SageMaker Canvas is the point-and-click, no-code way to build models and get predictions.

q: Which SageMaker capability helps create high-quality labelled training data, including with human labellers?
e: Ground Truth manages data labelling with human workforces and active learning.

q: Which SageMaker tool simplifies importing, cleaning and transforming data for ML, with a visual interface?
e: Data Wrangler handles data preparation and feature engineering visually.

q: Which SageMaker capability stores, shares and reuses ML features across teams and models?
e: Feature Store is a central repository for features used in training and inference.

q: Which SageMaker feature automatically tries algorithms and settings to build the best model from tabular data (AutoML)?
e: Autopilot automates model building, training and tuning, while still showing you how it did it.

q: Which SageMaker feature tracks model versions and approval status for deployment?
e: Model Registry catalogues model versions, metadata and approval status as part of MLOps.

q: A team needs to automate the steps of building, training and deploying models as a repeatable workflow. Which SageMaker feature fits?
e: SageMaker Pipelines orchestrates ML workflows (CI/CD for ML).

q: When is ML usually NOT the right solution?
o: When the problem has clear, fixed rules that give an exact answer
When there is a lot of historical data
When patterns are too complex to write by hand
When predictions need to improve over time
e: If simple deterministic rules solve it exactly and cheaply, ML adds cost and uncertainty for no benefit.
an: RPGACE's recall spacing (1, 3, 7, 16, 35 days) and the 2-click delete are plain rules. No model needed, and adding one would only add cost.
